title: Indian IT Stocks Shrug Off Wall Street Rout as Nifty IT Rises 2%
excerpt: Infosys, TCS and Mphasis led Indian IT higher on Friday morning even after US stocks posted their worst day since April 2025 in an AI-led sell-off.
body:
• Indian IT stocks rose on Friday morning, November 6, with the Nifty IT index up as much as 2.37% to 33,616.20, even as Wall Street suffered its worst day since April 2025.
  • On Thursday in the US, the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52% to 24,314.99, the S&P 500 fell 4.36% and the semiconductor index plunged 12%, its biggest drop since the start of the Covid pandemic.
  • Mphasis gained 4.46%, Infosys rose 1.58% to Rs 1,185.90 and TCS rose 1.79% to Rs 2,540.40 in early Mumbai trade, according to Upstox.
  • For diaspora investors: the move is a rotation story, not an all-clear — analysts cited by Moneycontrol earlier this week called the shift into IT services tactical and said the sector's earnings outlook had not fundamentally improved.

Indian technology services stocks opened higher on Friday, defying a severe overnight sell-off in the United States. The Nifty IT index jumped as much as 2.37% to 33,616.20 in opening deals, with nine of its 10 constituents in the green, Upstox reported. At 9:28 a.m. the index stood at 33,313.95, up 1.45% from its previous close of 32,837.85.

What happened on Wall Street

Thursday was the worst day for US stocks since April 2025, when President Donald Trump launched his tariff war, according to Dhanam Online's market report. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1,833.06 points, or 3.44%, to 51,523.06. The S&P 500 declined 334.89 points, or 4.36%, to 7,353.73, and the Nasdaq Composite plunged 1,421.52 points, or 5.52%, to 24,314.99. The seven largest technology companies lost around $1 trillion in market capitalisation in a single day, with Nvidia alone accounting for $440 billion of that erosion, the report said. For every stock that advanced, six declined, and the selling spread beyond technology to JPMorgan, Caterpillar and Boeing.

Why Indian IT moved the other way

Upstox attributed the divergence to what investors are calling an anti-AI trade: a rotation away from expensive AI-linked stocks toward traditional IT services companies. Indian IT firms are centred on technology services rather than AI hardware and infrastructure, and the Nifty IT index, among the worst-performing sectoral indices until September 2026, staged a sharp comeback in October and November. Foreign portfolio investors bought around Rs 6,463 crore worth of IT stocks during the September quarter, according to NSDL data cited in an October 22 report referenced by Upstox. Company results have also helped: TCS reported a 15% year-on-year increase in net profit, with total contract value of new deals at $9.6 billion for the second quarter of fiscal 2027.

American depositary receipts told a more mixed story on Thursday. Infosys ADRs surged 4.58% in regular trading but fell 2.50% in subsequent trading to close at $12.48, while Wipro was unchanged in regular trading and later declined 0.44% to $2.1505, Dhanam reported.

The caution from earlier this week

The same sector fell sharply only two days earlier. On Wednesday the Nifty IT index fell 2%, with TCS down around 3% and Infosys and Mphasis each down more than 2%, Moneycontrol reported. Sunny Agrawal, head of fundamental equity research at SBICAPS Securities, said then that the rotation into IT services was largely tactical and did not indicate a fundamental improvement in the earnings outlook, and that weakness in global AI stocks also raises questions about the sustainability of AI-led investment, including data-centre spending.

What to watch next

Asian markets extended the global sell-off on Friday morning, with Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi falling sharply at the open. Whether Mumbai's IT rally holds will depend on whether US technology stocks stabilise and on whether the rotation out of AI hardware continues. For now, the scoreboard is clear: the AI trade took its worst hit since 2020-era volatility, and Indian IT services — long treated as the stocks AI would disrupt — were where buyers went instead.
